item.passage:
[1] The summer I turned fifteen, my parents sent me to stay with my uncle Teodor, who ran a sign shop out of a garage in Marlow Falls. I had pictured computers and vinyl cutters. What I found instead was a long wooden bench a radio tuned to baseball, and rows of brushes standing in coffee cans like bouquets.

[2] Teodor painted every letter by hand, and at first I could not see why anyone paid him to. His customers could have bought printed banners for half the price: the bakery on Main Street, a family of beekeepers, a dentist who wanted his name in gold leaf. On my first morning I noticed that the jars of paint on the shelf above his bench was labeled in his own careful capitals, as if even his supplies deserved good lettering.

[3] He started me on the alphabet, I painted capital A's for three days. My first A's leaned like tired fence posts. Teodor would choose the least terrible in each row and circle it with a grease pencil. For two days I could not tell his circled letters from the rest. In other words, I began to see what he was choosing: the letters whose two strokes met cleanly at the peak and stood evenly on the line. A letter, he told me, stands the way a building does: if their base is crooked, nothing above it will look straight.

[4] By August, Teodor trusted me to repaint the bakery's front window, where the old gold letters had faded in the sun until they were barely visible and could hardly be seen. I traced their faint outlines onto paper before scraping the glass clean. Then I worked so slowly that the baker came out twice to ask whether I was still alive.

[5] By the end of the summer, I had lettered three customers' signs on my own: a truck door for the beekeepers, a price board for the hardware store, and a brass plaque for the dentist. Not one of them is perfect. Now, whenever I pass a hand-painted sign, I look first at the bottom of the letters. Checking, the way Teodor taught me, whether they stand evenly on the line. Usually I can tell which painters had someone circling the good ones.

choices: No Change
alphabet, and I painted

alphabet, then I painted
item.correct_answer: alphabet, and I painted

item.passage:
Transcript: Today, we’re going to discuss the concept of plate tectonics and its significance in geology. Why does this matter? Well, understanding plate tectonics helps us predict natural disasters and explains the distribution of continents and oceans. But it also provides insight into Earth’s history and the processes that shape our planet’s surface over millions of years. The theory of plate tectonics proposes that Earth’s outer shell, called the lithosphere, is divided into several large and small plates that move over the semi-fluid asthenosphere beneath them. These plates are constantly shifting, although usually at rates of just a few centimeters per year. For example, the Pacific Plate is moving northwest at about 7 centimeters per year, which is why the San Andreas Fault in California experiences frequent earthquakes. This movement isn’t just theoretical—what researchers have found is that GPS measurements can now track these shifts with remarkable accuracy, sometimes down to a few millimeters per year. The interesting thing here is that this technology has confirmed what geologists had hypothesized long before such precise tools were available. Now, let’s talk about plate boundaries. There are three main types: divergent, convergent, and transform.

At divergent boundaries, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates move apart and new crust forms as magma rises from below. This is known as a constructive boundary. For instance, Iceland sits atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is actually growing a little bit each year as new land is created. On the other hand, convergent boundaries are where plates move toward each other. A key process here is subduction, where one plate slides beneath another. In the Andes Mountains, the Nazca Plate is subducting under the South American Plate, leading to volcanic activity, earthquakes, and mountain formation. I should clarify—not all plate boundaries are destructive. Some, like the Himalayas, are formed when two continental plates collide, crumpling up rather than subducting, which leads to the creation of massive mountain ranges. As an aside, it’s important to note that plate tectonics also helps explain phenomena like the distribution of fossils and minerals, as well as the occurrence of tsunamis and volcanic eruptions. So, in conclusion, plate tectonics is not just a theoretical model—it’s a comprehensive framework that helps us understand, and even anticipate, geological events. This is crucial for public safety, urban planning, and ongoing scientific research, allowing us to better prepare for and respond to natural hazards.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Plate Tectonics] What can be inferred about Iceland from the lecture?
choices: It formed where two continental plates crumpled together
Its land area increases because new crust is being created beneath it
It sits above a subduction zone, which accounts for its volcanic activity
It is at risk because the Pacific Plate is moving northwest beneath it
item.correct_answer: Its land area increases because new crust is being created beneath it

item.passage: Transcript: Okay, so today I want to talk about the Impressionists, and I want you to set aside the idea that they were just, you know, painters of pretty gardens. What was actually radical about them was a shift in what a painting was supposed to be for. Before them, the studio was king. You'd sketch outside, sure, but the real picture got built indoors, layer by layer, smoothed down until the brushstrokes disappeared. The Impressionists basically inverted that. What researchers of the period found is that they treated the finished-looking, blended surface as almost a lie about how we actually see. So Monet, Pissarro, they'd haul their paints outdoors and try to get the whole thing down in one session, chasing a particular quality of light before it changed. That's why you get those loose, visible dabs of color — not sloppiness, but a record of speed. And here's an aside: this only became practical because paint started being sold in metal tubes, so you could carry it. Now, the critics hated it at first. The very name 'Impressionism' was an insult — a reviewer sneering that these were mere impressions, not real paintings. But that's exactly the point. They weren't after the permanent thing; they were after the moment.
item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Art History] What can be inferred about the origin of the term 'Impressionism'?
choices: It was chosen by the painters themselves as a proud label.
It began as a critic's insult that captured what the movement valued.
It referred to the metal tubes the painters carried.
It was coined decades after the movement had ended.
item.correct_answer: It began as a critic's insult that captured what the movement valued.

item.passage:
The Impressionist movement in art history, which emerged in France during the late nineteenth century, is often celebrated for its innovative use of light and color. Many artists of this movement, such as Monet and Renoir, sought to capture fleeting moments and the transient effects of sunlight on their subjects. However, some critics at the time dismissed Impressionism as unfinished or overly spontaneous, arguing that its loose brushwork lacked the discipline of traditional academic painting. Paradoxically, this very spontaneity became a hallmark of the movement, influencing generations of artists.

In most cases, Impressionists painted outdoors, a practice known as 'en plein air,' to better observe natural light. This approach contrasted sharply with the studio-based methods favored by earlier artists. The cause-effect relationship between technological advances—such as the invention of portable paint tubes—and the rise of outdoor painting is widely acknowledged. While many Impressionists focused on landscapes, others explored urban scenes, reflecting the rapidly changing environment of modern Paris. Despite initial resistance, Impressionism eventually gained acceptance and is now regarded as a pivotal development in the history of Western art.
item.prompt: [Academic — Art History] What is the author's central claim about the Impressionist movement?
choices: Impressionism was universally accepted by critics from the moment its paintings were first shown in Paris.
Traditional academic painting was superior to Impressionist technique, which critics rightly dismissed as undisciplined and unfinished.
The Impressionist movement focused only on rural landscapes painted outdoors, away from the changing city.
Impressionism's innovative techniques and focus on spontaneity ultimately transformed Western art despite initial criticism.
item.correct_answer: Impressionism's innovative techniques and focus on spontaneity ultimately transformed Western art despite initial criticism.

item.passage:
[1] Most flowering plants bloom on a calendar set by the seasons. A few bamboo species keep a different clock. One timber bamboo grown across East Asia flowers roughly once every 120 years, and when it does, nearly every plant in the world's scattered stands flower within a year or two of the others, whether it grows on a hillside in China or in a botanical garden on another continent.

[2] For centuries the pattern puzzled botanists, because the plants seem to have no way of signaling one another across oceans. Most researchers now think the timing is internal: each plant carries a kind of counter that began running when its parent stand last flowered. Bamboo spreads mainly through underground stems, so the plants in a forest are often clones of a single ancestor. They share a starting date. Nevertheless, they reach the end of the count together.

[3] What follows the flowering is as dramatic as the flowering itself. A stand produces an enormous crop of seed then it dies, often across hundreds of square miles at once. In northeastern India, one species flowers about every 48 years, and the flood of seed sets off a population explosion among rats. When the seed is gone, the rats turn to the farmers rice fields, and famine has followed several of these flowerings.

[4] Why would a plant wait so long and then spend everything at once? The most widely accepted explanation, first proposed by an ecologist in the 1970s, is that the strategy overwhelms the animals that eat seeds. If a bamboo released a little seed every year, mice, birds, and wild pigs could scarf down pretty much all of it. By flooding the ground with more seed than any population of seed-eaters can consume the plants ensure that some seeds survive to sprout.

[5] The long gap does its own work. Waiting decades kept the seed-eaters scarce between flowerings, so no large population is standing ready when the next crop arrives. A bamboo that flowered every few years would be feeding its enemies; one that waits a century is ambushing them.
item.prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Most researchers now think the timing is internal: each plant carries a kind of counter that began running when its parent stand last flowered," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "internal: each"?
choices: No Change
internal, each
internal each
internal, with each
item.correct_answer: No Change
